lesson.text: Quick memory: what is a procedure? (A group of steps with a name.) Today: building on someone else's program or picture, the fair way.
A remix takes someone's work, a program, a song or a picture, and changes it into something new: new rules, new pictures, a new ending.
People own what they make. Before you remix, check that the creator allows it. Many creators share their work on purpose, with a licence that says what others may do with it.
Give credit: say who made the original and where it came from. 'Based on Balloon Pop by Juno' tells everyone whose idea it was, and it thanks her.
Worked example: Zara remixes Bram's maze game. She adds a key and a locked door, and writes: 'Remix of Bram's Maze. I added the key and the door.' Now everyone knows which parts are hers.

lines: WHEN the key is picked up

lesson.text: Taking someone's work and saying you made it all is not fair, even if you change a little. It hides their work and takes the thanks that belong to them.
This game does it too. Its sounds and pictures come from creators who gave them away freely (CC0). Its list of credits names them, to say thank you.
Try it in the world: with a friend's permission, remix one of their builds: change three things, then put up a sign that credits them and says what you changed. Next: how messages travel.

exercises.prompt: A remix changes someone's work into something new.
exercises.hint: Think of Zara's maze with a key and a door.
exercises.explain: True: a remix starts from someone's work and changes it into something new.

exercises.prompt: What should you do when you share a remix?
exercises.hint: Whose idea was the first version?
choices: Say you made all of it
exercises.explain: Credit the creator: say who made the original and where it came from.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: fair, or not fair?
exercises.hint: Would the creator feel thanked, or would their work be hidden?
exercises.explain: Credit, asking first and saying what you changed are fair. Claiming it all and cutting off their name are not.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
matches: change a work into a new one
exercises.explain: A remix changes a work, credit says who made it, a licence says what others may do, the original is the start.

exercises.hint: A good credit names the creator and says what you changed.
choices: Remix of Mimi's Space Race; I added a moon
exercises.explain: It names Mimi, names her game, and says what the remix added.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of a fair remix in order.
exercises.hint: Check before you change anything, and credit before you share.
items: Credit them and say what you changed
Find a work you may remix
exercises.explain: Find a work, check what is allowed, make your changes, credit the creator and your changes, then share.

exercises.prompt: If you change a few things in someone's program, it becomes all your own work.
exercises.hint: Who wrote the parts you did not change?
exercises.explain: False: most of it is still their work, so you credit them and say what you changed.

exercises.prompt: Bram's game adds 1 point for each gem. What did Zara change in her remix?
exercises.hint: Compare her line with Bram's: CHANGE score BY 1.
choices: Each gem is now worth 5 points
exercises.explain: Her remix says CHANGE score BY 5, so each gem is worth 5 points instead of 1.

lines: WHEN a gem is picked up

exercises.prompt: Tilly finds a song online with no creator's name and no licence. What should she do before using it in her game?
exercises.hint: Not knowing who made it doesn't mean nobody did.
choices: Find out who made it and if she may use it
Use it and say she wrote it
Change one note and call it hers
exercises.explain: Someone made it, so Tilly finds out who and whether she may use it, or chooses music shared for everyone.

exercises.prompt: Pip says Juno may use his drawing if she credits him. What should Juno do?
exercises.explain: Pip allows it with credit, so Juno uses it and names Pip.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: does it help the original creator, or hurt them?
exercises.explain: Credits, links and thanks help creators. Passing it off, cutting their name and selling without asking hurt them.

exercises.prompt: CC0 means the creator gave the work to everyone, to use even without credit, but a credit is still kind.
exercises.hint: Think of the sounds and pictures in this game.
exercises.explain: True: CC0 gives the work away for any use; this game still names its creators to thank them.

exercises.prompt: Why do programmers say what they changed in a remix?
exercises.hint: Think of Zara's note about the key and the door.
choices: So everyone knows which parts are theirs
exercises.explain: Saying what changed shows which parts are yours and which are the original creator's.

exercises.prompt: Match each problem to the fair fix.
items: not sure you may use it
exercises.hint: What would make each one fair?
exercises.explain: No credit: add their name. Not sure: ask. People think it's all yours: say what you changed. A bug: tell them kindly.
